articles.title: New York sends $189 million to close the summer hunger gap
articles.summary:

The post New York sends $189 million to close the summer hunger gap first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Here’s some food for thought: for students, free lunch ends when school does. For the millions of children who rely on subsidized cafeteria meals during the year, nothing automatically fills that gap in June. On July 1, Governor Kathy Hochul announced that $189 million in Summer Electronic Benefits Transfer funds had already reached nearly 1.6 million low-income children across the state, with roughly $240 million projected to reach around 2 million kids before the season is out.

A USDA demonstration project found that summer food benefits cut the share of children experiencing very low food security by one-third. Summer hunger doesn’t get much coverage. That number suggests it probably should.

How New York’s Summer EBT program works

Each eligible child gets $120 on an EBT card that works like SNAP at authorized grocery stores and farmers markets. Families already enrolled in SNAP, Public Assistance, or Medicaid get it automatically, with no application. Families not automatically enrolled have until September 8, 2026 to apply online at ny.gov/SummerEBT.

Important to note: the $120 expires 122 days after it’s issued, and any unused balance disappears once that window closes. Families should use it soon after the card arrives. To qualify, a child must attend a school that participates in the National School Lunch Program and meet the income thresholds for free or reduced-price meals.

What child hunger advocates are saying

Joel Berg, CEO of Hunger Free America, named the core problem: children who get school meals during the year “don’t receive government-funded food at summer meals sites when schools are closed.” Richard R. Buery Jr., CEO of Robin Hood, described summer as a time when “school meals disappear and budgets are stretched thin” for low-income families across the state. Both were making the same basic point: the gap is structural, and it opens every year on the same date.

The EBT spending also moves through neighborhoods. No Kid Hungry New York Director Rachel Sabella noted that the dollars “strengthen local economies by allowing recipients to spend them at neighborhood grocery stores, farmers markets, and other local businesses.” Assemblymember Maritza Davila, chair of the Assembly Social Services Committee, described families already “struggling with the rising cost of everything in their lives from housing, medical care and especially food costs,” with summer adding more weight to that load.

A state commitment as federal nutrition cuts loom

Federal nutrition programs are facing Republican-backed cuts in Congress. Senator Charles Schumer called federal funding for hungry children “more critical than ever,” citing reductions he said are already taking effect. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who pushed to make the federal Summer EBT program permanent, described New York’s program as a direct response to that federal retreat.

New York’s FY27 budget went well beyond the EBT rollout. Hochul secured $51 million for the Hunger Prevention and Nutrition Assistance Program, $15 million to expand it to regional food banks and pantries, and $55 million for the Nourish NY program, plus $395 million to continue Universal Free School Meals through fiscal year 2027. Kate Breslin of the Schuyler Center for Analysis and Advocacy cited a Federal Reserve Bank of New York finding of “a remarkable increase in food insecurity, particularly among households with young children.” Families who haven’t received their benefits yet have until September 8, 2026, to apply.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

It includes detailed context on program mechanics, advocacy perspectives, and broader budget commitments, demonstrating meaningful and substantive progress in combating child hunger and food insecurity.
articles.personality_title: New York invests $189 million to fight summer hunger for children
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many children in New York rely on free or reduced-price school meals during the school year. However, when summer arrives and schools close, these meals stop, leaving a gap where many children may not get enough food.

**What happened** – On July 1, Governor Kathy Hochul announced that New York has distributed $189 million through the Summer Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) program. This money has already helped nearly 1.6 million low-income children buy food at grocery stores and farmers markets. The state expects to send about $240 million total to around 2 million children by the end of summer.

**Impact** – The Summer EBT program gives each eligible child $120 on a card to spend on food. This helps reduce hunger during the summer when school meals are not available. A study showed that summer food benefits can reduce very low food security for children by one-third. Besides helping families, the program also supports local businesses where families shop.

**What's next step** – Families who qualify but have not yet received benefits can apply online until September 8, 2026. Meanwhile, New York is also increasing funding for other nutrition programs and free school meals to help more families throughout the year.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New York’s $189 million Summer EBT program is a strong step to close the summer food gap for millions of children who depend on school meals.

articles.personality_title_es: Nueva York destina 189 millones de dólares para combatir el hambre infantil en verano
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchos niños en Nueva York dependen de comidas escolares gratuitas o a precio reducido durante el año escolar. Pero cuando llega el verano y las escuelas cierran, estas comidas se detienen, dejando un vacío donde muchos niños pueden quedarse sin suficiente alimento.

**Qué pasó** – El 1 de julio, la gobernadora Kathy Hochul anunció que Nueva York ha distribuido 189 millones de dólares a través del programa Summer Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT). Este dinero ya ha ayudado a cerca de 1.6 millones de niños de bajos ingresos a comprar comida en supermercados y mercados locales. El estado espera enviar unos 240 millones en total a alrededor de 2 millones de niños para el final del verano.

**Impacto** – El programa Summer EBT entrega a cada niño elegible 120 dólares en una tarjeta para comprar alimentos. Esto ayuda a reducir el hambre durante el verano, cuando no hay comidas escolares. Un estudio mostró que estos beneficios reducen en un tercio la inseguridad alimentaria grave entre los niños. Además de ayudar a las familias, el programa también apoya a los negocios locales donde las familias compran.

**Próximo paso** – Las familias que califican pero aún no han recibido beneficios pueden solicitar en línea hasta el 8 de septiembre de 2026. Mientras tanto, Nueva York también está aumentando el financiamiento para otros programas de nutrición y comidas escolares gratuitas para ayudar a más familias durante todo el año.

**Frase clave** – El programa Summer EBT de 189 millones de dólares de Nueva York es un paso importante para cerrar la brecha alimentaria de verano para millones de niños que dependen de las comidas escolares.

articles.title: What does home mean for people with no single territory connecting them?
articles.summary: In this collaborative article, Global Voices contributors explore these two stories of statelessness, and reveal how minority communities are redefining nationhood, loyalty, and identity across the region.
articles.content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ July 2026 Spotlight series, “Statelessness.” This series offers insight into the issue of statelessness and how it hinders people’s freedom of movement, educational opportunities, political access, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.

While trying to define nationhood, people often rely on simplistic descriptions and groupings — the lines drawn on a map, demarcations outlined by treaties and agreements, common identities and ideologies within a specific space — but for many people groups, the concept of nationhood can fall outside these traditional borders. This is the case for many in post-Soviet spaces, for example, Ukraine’s Roma community, whose members are now fighting Russia and dying for a country that, for generations, treated them as outsiders. It is also true for Tatars, whose homeland largely exists within a cultural space rather than a physical one.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, hundreds of Roma have joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine in the fight against Russia. Yet despite this service, Roma Ukrainian refugees continue facing discrimination within Ukraine and beyond in Europe.

Further east, within Russia, Tatars, the country’s second-largest ethnic group, continue to grapple with a different question: What does homeland mean for a people scattered across continents, with no single territory uniting them? Tatarstan, a republic of the Russian Federation, remains a cultural anchor, but for many Tatars, belonging is carried through community and culture rather than a location on a map. That dispersion, together with a traumatic, fraught history, shapes how Tatars today navigate conversations about sovereignty, separatism, and self-determination.

In this collaborative article, Global Voices contributors explore these two stories of statelessness and reveal how minority communities are redefining nationhood, loyalty, and identity across the region.

The Ukrainian Roma fighting Russia, yet still not accepted

Since the second Russian large-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, there have been few stories of Ukraine’s Roma population fighting for Ukraine, even as many took to the front lines.

Already in 2022, Roma journalist Viktor Chovka reported that Roma soldiers were fighting within the Ukrainian Army because they were born in Ukraine and considered it their home.

Myroslav Horvat, another Romani activist in Ukraine, told Swedish Radio Romano at that time that most Romani people were concerned about how they would make a living because they lost their jobs when the war began. On his Facebook profile, Horvat often shares photographs of Romani soldiers in the Ukrainian Army. His main photo also features the Ukrainian flag, highlighting the dual identities that many Ukrainian Roma carry.

According to Horvat, approximately 250 Roma from Zakarpattia joined Ukraine’s defense forces in 2022. By August 2024, he estimated that more than 500 were serving. Ukrainian flags have become increasingly visible in Roma settlements, alongside greater use of the Ukrainian language and Ukrainian songs.

In an article from 2024 by the Ukrainian media outlet Varosh, Horvat said Roma people historically lived as minorities under various states and empires and rarely occupied secure social positions. Their experience of persecution during the Second World War also contributed to a historical distance from military institutions. Today, however, many equate defending Ukraine to defending their own families and future.

Horvat also mentions educational inequality: He estimates that around 40 percent of Roma in Zakarpattia, Ukraine, lack a basic secondary education, although the situation has improved in recent years. Some Roma have never obtained Ukrainian passports, which can prevent them from being formally mobilized. Regional recruitment officials say low literacy does not necessarily prevent military service, but it can create practical difficulties.

Anti-Discrimination Center “Memorial” organized a meeting in 2025 in Brussels with Roma veterans who voluntarily joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine, where Roma veterans described both discrimination and solidarity within the Ukrainian armed forces.

Roma Arsen Mednyk joined the military after Russian forces occupied his hometown, Bucha, and massacred civilians there. Initially treated with suspicion because he was Roma, he earned the trust of other soldiers and later became a storm-unit commander. His story was presented in a documentary about Roma soldiers and the war.

Marginalization and discrimination of Roma refugees

Before February 2022, Ukraine’s Roma population already faced severe barriers to citizenship, housing, education, healthcare, and employment.

Of an estimated 400,000 Roma living in the country, around 30,000 reportedly lacked official identity documents, leaving them functionally stateless. Roma women sometimes gave birth at home because of discrimination or unaffordable medical costs, leaving children without birth certificates and forcing families to live at the margins of society. Roma communities were also sometimes targeted by nationalist groups and were often the victims of discrimination and prejudice.

After the Russian invasion, discrimination followed Roma families to Ukraine’s borders. Human rights organizations received reports of unequal treatment, including a case of a mother and two children who were repeatedly prevented from crossing into Hungary.

In European reception centers, Roma refugees were sometimes segregated from other Ukrainians. In Moldova, families were placed in facilities without adequate heating or hot water. In the Czech Republic, the Guardian reported in 2022, Roma slept in poor conditions at Prague’s railway station and were accused of pretending to be Ukrainian to obtain assistance. Volunteers also reported that some hosts in Moldova and Poland were willing to accommodate only white refugees, while the Roma are widely considered people of color.

For some families, the hostility was so intense that they chose to return to war-torn Ukraine rather than remain in discriminatory conditions.

For Tatars, homeland is more than a place on the map

While the war has pushed many Ukrainian Roma to defend a land they consider theirs, for Tatars, however, the relationship between identity and territory has never been so simple.

Tatars are the second-largest ethnic nation in the Russian Federation, yet there is no single place that all Tatars call home. The Republic of Tatarstan, a territory within Russia, is often described as the homeland of the Tatars, but ethnic Tatars make up only around half of the republic’s population, sharing it with Russians, Bashkirs, Chuvash, Armenians and many others.

Beyond Tatarstan, millions of Tatars live across Russia, in neighboring republics, oblasts, krais and major cities, as well as throughout the post-Soviet space and in diasporas across Europe, Türkiye, North America and beyond. Some communities were formed through centuries of imperial expansion, forced resettlement and Soviet policies, while others emerged through education, work or personal choice. As a result, Tatar identity has long existed across borders rather than within them.

This dispersion has shaped how many Tatars understand belonging. Tatarstan remains the historical and cultural center of the nation, home to institutions that preserve the language, literature, and traditions. But for many Tatars, “homeland” is just as likely to be found around a family table, through the Tatar language, music, Sabantuy celebrations or even the ritual of sharing tea as it is on a map. The culture has become the thread connecting communities separated by geography, politics and generations. For a people spread across continents, identity is often carried rather than inherited from a single place.

This also explains why conversations about the future of Tatarstan often sound different inside Tatar communities than they do abroad. Previous attempts to link Tatar national aspirations to geopolitical projects, including the German-sponsored Idel-Ural Legion during World War II and the collaboration of some Crimean Tatar groups with Nazi occupation authorities, were followed by devastating consequences, most notably the collective deportation of the Crimean Tatars in 1944.

These episodes continue to influence how many Tatars perceive questions of sovereignty and separatism. Some commentators, including contributors regularly featured by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), the Idel-Ural project, and affiliated platforms, have argued that Russia’s republics should become independent states if the Russian Federation were ever to disintegrate.

Yet such discussions do not necessarily reflect the views of many Tatars themselves.

With Tatars living across the Russian Federation and far beyond its borders, and with Tatarstan located in the geographical heart of European Russia rather than on its periphery, the republic holds a significance that is primarily historical, cultural, and symbolic. For many Tatars, as for other minorities in Russia, preserving language, culture and community remains a more immediate concern than redrawing political borders.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the inspiring resilience and identity preservation of stateless minority communities, particularly the Ukrainian Roma fighting for their country despite discrimination, and the Tatars maintaining cultural cohesion across dispersed populations. It addresses significant human rights issues such as statelessness, discrimination, and cultural survival with detailed context, showing real-world impact and broad societal relevance.
articles.personality_title: How Ukrainian Roma and Tatars redefine home and identity beyond borders
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people think of a nation as a clear place on a map with shared culture and laws. But some groups, like the Ukrainian Roma and Tatars in Russia, don’t fit this idea because they are spread out or face discrimination. This story is part of a series exploring statelessness, which means not having official citizenship or a clear homeland.

**What happened** – Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, hundreds of Ukrainian Roma have joined the fight for their country even though they face discrimination and lack some official documents. Meanwhile, Tatars, Russia’s second-largest ethnic group, live scattered across many places with no single territory that all Tatars call home. They keep their culture alive through language, music, and traditions rather than a specific location.

**Impact** – Ukrainian Roma soldiers show courage by defending a country that has often treated them as outsiders, highlighting their strong connection to Ukraine despite challenges. At the same time, Tatars demonstrate that a shared culture and community can be stronger than a shared land. Both groups challenge traditional ideas of nationhood and show how identity and belonging can exist beyond borders.

**What's next step** – The stories of these communities encourage more attention to issues like statelessness, discrimination, and cultural survival. Efforts may increase to support minority rights, improve access to education and citizenship, and preserve cultural traditions. Understanding these experiences could influence how countries and organizations help stateless and dispersed peoples in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Ukrainian Roma fighting for their country and Tatars preserving culture across lands show that home and identity go beyond borders and official maps.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment les Roms ukrainiens et les Tatars redéfinissent le foyer et l'identité au-delà des frontières
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup pensent qu'une nation est un lieu clair sur une carte avec une culture et des lois communes. Mais certains groupes, comme les Roms ukrainiens et les Tatars en Russie, ne correspondent pas à cette idée car ils sont dispersés ou subissent des discriminations. Cette histoire fait partie d'une série sur l'apatridie, c’est-à-dire le fait de ne pas avoir de citoyenneté officielle ou de foyer clair.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Depuis l'invasion russe de l'Ukraine en 2022, des centaines de Roms ukrainiens ont rejoint la lutte pour leur pays malgré les discriminations et l'absence de certains documents officiels. Pendant ce temps, les Tatars, deuxième groupe ethnique de Russie, vivent dispersés dans de nombreux endroits sans territoire unique que tous les Tatars considèrent comme leur foyer. Ils maintiennent leur culture vivante grâce à la langue, la musique et les traditions plutôt qu'à un lieu précis.

**Impact** – Les soldats Roms ukrainiens montrent du courage en défendant un pays qui les a souvent traités comme des étrangers, soulignant leur fort lien avec l’Ukraine malgré les difficultés. En même temps, les Tatars démontrent qu'une culture et une communauté partagées peuvent être plus fortes qu'une terre commune. Ces deux groupes remettent en question les idées traditionnelles de la nation et montrent que l'identité peut exister au-delà des frontières.

**Prochaine étape** – Ces histoires encouragent une plus grande attention aux problèmes comme l'apatridie, la discrimination et la survie culturelle. Il pourrait y avoir plus d'efforts pour soutenir les droits des minorités, améliorer l'accès à l'éducation et à la citoyenneté, et préserver les traditions culturelles. Comprendre ces expériences pourrait influencer la manière dont les pays et les organisations aident les peuples apatrides et dispersés à l'avenir.

**Phrase clé** – Les Roms ukrainiens qui défendent leur pays et les Tatars qui préservent leur culture à travers les terres montrent que le foyer et l'identité vont au-delà des frontières et des cartes officielles.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo los romaníes ucranianos y los tártaros redefinen el hogar y la identidad más allá de las fronteras
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas piensan que una nación es un lugar claro en un mapa con cultura y leyes compartidas. Pero algunos grupos, como los romaníes ucranianos y los tártaros en Rusia, no encajan en esta idea porque están dispersos o enfrentan discriminación. Esta historia forma parte de una serie sobre apatridia, que significa no tener ciudadanía oficial o un hogar claro.

**Qué pasó** – Desde la invasión rusa a Ucrania en 2022, cientos de romaníes ucranianos se han unido a la defensa de su país a pesar de la discriminación y la falta de algunos documentos oficiales. Mientras tanto, los tártaros, el segundo grupo étnico más grande de Rusia, viven dispersos en muchos lugares sin un territorio único que todos consideren su hogar. Mantienen viva su cultura a través del idioma, la música y las tradiciones, en lugar de un lugar específico.

**Impacto** – Los soldados romaníes ucranianos muestran valentía al defender un país que a menudo los ha tratado como extranjeros, destacando su fuerte conexión con Ucrania a pesar de las dificultades. Al mismo tiempo, los tártaros demuestran que una cultura y comunidad compartidas pueden ser más fuertes que una tierra común. Ambos grupos desafían las ideas tradicionales de nación y muestran que la identidad puede existir más allá de las fronteras.

**Próximo paso** – Estas historias fomentan una mayor atención a problemas como la apatridia, la discriminación y la supervivencia cultural. Es probable que aumenten los esfuerzos para apoyar los derechos de las minorías, mejorar el acceso a la educación y la ciudadanía, y preservar las tradiciones culturales. Comprender estas experiencias podría influir en cómo los países y organizaciones ayudan a los pueblos apátridas y dispersos en el futuro.

**Frase clave** – Los romaníes ucranianos que luchan por su país y los tártaros que preservan su cultura a través de tierras muestran que el hogar y la identidad van más allá de las fronteras y los mapas oficiales.
